newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists suffer worst-ever defeat.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists suffer worst-ever defeat.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling former communists suffered the worst defeat of their six-year history in weekend presidential elections, official preliminary results showed on Monday.

Frustrated by falling living standards and worried about looming food and fuel shortages, the 6.75 million voters of this ex-Soviet satellite gave opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov a clear -- if not decisive -- victory.
Stoyanov was leading with 43.65 percent of the vote, according to the electoral commission, with his Socialist rival Ivan Marazov trailing second with 27.07 percent.
Final results are due on Wednesday.
Since neither gained an absolute majority, the two front-runners now face a deciding round on November 3, which Stoyanov has predicted he will win.

The ultimate outcome of Bulgaria's second presidential election since the 1989 fall of communism will depend, candidates agree, on the 22 percent of voters who cast their ballots for third-placed candidate George Ganchev.
Stoyanov has hailed the result as a big change in Bulgarian voting patterns and told reporters Ganchev's supporters would now swing behind his Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).
"The vote shows a new majority is being formed," he told his triumphant supporters on Sunday night.
Ganchev himself has said he will not back either of the run-off candidates.
Monday's newspapers described Stoyanov's lead as a stinging blow to the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) government.
"There is no winner but we know who the loser is," said Troud daily, while Kontinent newspaper noted: "The BSP has lost elections before but never by such a wide margin."
The BSP is predominantly made up of former communists who hastily renamed themselves socialists after the fall of dictator Todor Zhivkov.
BSP Prime Minister Zhan Videnov has a secure majority in parliament -- where real power in Bulgaria lies -- while the more ceremonial post of president is already held by the opposition UDF.
But political analysts expect the latest result to widen splits within the Socialists and increase pressure for an early parliamentary election.
They doubt, however, whether it will do much to solve Bulgaria's dire economic woes.
Of all the east-European former Warsaw Pact countries, Bulgaria has made the least progress towards shaking off its communist legacy, economists say.
While its former allies line up for membership of organisations like the EU and NATO, Sofia often seems to be looking more towards Moscow than Brussels.
It has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.
The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and wheat to prevent shortages during the coming winter.
Prices are rising, interest rates are up around 240 percent and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago.
All now depends, economists agree, on the International Monetary Fund's agreeing to release a twice-delayed $115 million credit to allow the country to stave off default on its foreign debt.
